failures.criterion: 2. The comment is created and anchored to the selected text (plan acceptance 2), and the rule the INFRA-512 architect's decisions rest on: a record on a passage the reader never selected is worse than a refusal, because no refusal ever tells them about it
failures.evidence: When another writer deletes the sentence the reader's own words were in, and the block still reads those words once somewhere else, the comment is attached to that other reading. Red test: packages/dispatch/e2e/compose-wait.e2e.ts, 'a comment is not moved to the block's other reading when its own words are deleted' (commit 6b2682c2e2b5). Paragraph 'Alpha the lazy dog. Beta the lazy dog.'; the reader selects the second reading (offset 25); another writer rewrites the paragraph to 'Alpha the lazy dog.', taking both the mark and the reader's own sentence. Measured: the comment is created and its mark sits at offset 6 - 'Alpha the lazy dog', the reading the reader never selected - and the composer closes, so nothing is said. The red row asserts the only correct outcome here, since the reader's passage is gone: no comment row, the draft kept, the composer showing it, and no mark left in the document. It fails at the implementer's head with 'Your draft is kept' not found, because the composer has closed on a sent comment. Mechanism, read in packages/proof-editor/src/record-mark-retype.ts remarkRange: when no reading in the remembered block matches the remembered surroundings, the block's only reading of the quote is taken anyway - the asymmetry the implementer's handoff records as deliberate, which keeps the sentence-rewrite row green. It cannot tell that row's case (the reader's words still there, the words around them rewritten) from this one (the reader's words deleted, somebody else's reading left). The INFRA-512 architect set this break attempt and said to fail the round on this outcome and decide the rule with both rows in hand; the surroundings of the remaining reading are evidence it could use, as is how many readings the block held when the mark was written.

verifiedAtThisHead: Break attempt, a reading at the very start of its block (empty prefix): correct. 'the lazy dog sits here and the lazy dog sits there.', the reader on the first reading, another writer rewriting the tail to 'sits yonder' and taking the mark: the comment lands on reading 0, the reader's own. An empty prefix matches every reading, so the suffix alone separates them here, and it does.

Break attempt, a reading at the very end of its block (empty suffix): correct. The reader on the trailing reading of 'Once upon a time there was a hound and the lazy dog sits here and then the lazy dog', another writer rewriting the opening outside the remembered 32 characters: the comment follows the reader's words to their new offset (71 → 76) and stays the last reading.

Break attempt, two readings whose surroundings are identical too: correct, it refuses. A paragraph of 'the lazy dog sits. ' nine times over, the reader on reading 4, where four readings carry the same 32 characters on each side: no comment is created, no mark is left, the draft 'Which dog is this?' stays in the field, and the composer says the words are still in the document but no longer where they were selected. My first attempt at this row, with the sentence five times over, was inconclusive and is not evidence: the block was too short for a second reading to carry a full 32 characters on both sides, so one reading matched and the comment was placed correctly.

Break attempt, the reader's passage moved to another block: correct. 'Alpha the lazy dog sits here.' replaced by 'Nothing of the sort.' while the same sentence is written into a third paragraph, with a decoy reading ('Beta the lazy dog sits there.') standing throughout: the comment attaches in the paragraph the sentence moved to and nowhere else.

Break attempt, a word inside the remembered prefix edited while the selected words are untouched ('Beta' → 'Bravo' in 'Alpha the lazy dog. Beta the lazy dog.'): it refuses and keeps the draft, which is the safe answer with two readings and no surroundings to tell them apart. What the reader is told is not quite true: 'The text you selected is still in the document, but no longer where you selected it' - the words are exactly where they were selected; it is the word in front of them that changed. Worth a truer sentence for this case while the wording is open anyway, not a failure of its own.
